concept.name: Retracement
concept.definition: A temporary reversal within a larger trend that gives back only part of the prior move before the trend resumes. The term is magnitude-focused — how much of the prior leg was retraced — and is usually measured in percentages (e.g., Fibonacci levels); it describes structure, not a prediction of resumption.
concept.intuition: The market gives back a slice of what it just gained, then carries on — the question is always how big the slice will be.
concept.mechanics: Measured as a percentage of the prior swing: retracement level = pivot high - (retracement % x (pivot high - pivot low)) for a pullback in an up-leg. Shallow retracements (~38.2%) are read as trend strength, deep ones (~61.8%-78.6%) as potential weakness or reversal risk.
concept.formula: Retracement level = High - r x (High - Low) for an up-leg, where r is the retracement fraction (e.g., 0.382, 0.5, 0.618); symmetrically Low + r x (High - Low) for a down-leg.
concept.failure_modes: There is no level a retracement must respect; a 'retracement' that exceeds 100% of the prior leg was in fact a reversal, which is only clear afterward.
concept.misconceptions: That price is likely to stop at a particular retracement percentage; the percentages are observation conventions, and prices break through them regularly.
concept.example: After a rally from 5809 to 6162 in S&P 500 futures, a decline to 5944 is a 61.8% retracement of the up-leg (6162.25 - 0.618 x 353.25 = 5944).
